reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# mdview packaging & distribution: practices report

## 1. Stack & distribution channels
- **Stack:** a Rust workspace (`Cargo.toml`) with `mdview-core` (library) and `mdview` (the CLI binary). A Tauri desktop crate is left out of the default build (`Cargo.toml:4-6`) so the CLI never needs webview libraries. There is one version for everything, `[workspace.package] version = "0.8.11"`. Release profile: `opt-level="s"`, `lto`, `codegen-units=1`, `panic="abort"`, `strip`.
- **Channels:**
  - GitHub Releases: raw binaries, one per target.
  - `curl … install.sh | sh` for Unix and `irm … install.ps1 | iex` for Windows.
  - `cargo install --git` as the fallback.
  - The built-in `mdview update` command.
- **Not used:** crates.io, Homebrew, Scoop, winget, distro packages, Docker.
- **Front-end assets are committed and embedded at compile time.** `tools/codemirror-bundle/package.json` is an esbuild build whose output gets committed, so a Rust build never needs Node.

## 2. Area by area

### Build / release
- **CI** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): `cargo fmt --check`, `clippy -D warnings` and `test --workspace` on Ubuntu, plus a separate test job on Windows.
- **Release** (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) runs when a `v*` tag is pushed (or by manual dispatch).
  - The matrix builds `x86_64/aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` (via `cross`, giving static binaries that run on any distro), `aarch64-apple-darwin` on `macos-14`, and `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.
  - Intel macOS was dropped on purpose. The comment at `:28-31` says the scarce runner kept stalling releases, and Intel Macs fall back to building with cargo.
  - `fail-fast: false`, and the Rust cache is keyed per target.
- **Asset naming:** a flat name with no archive, `mdview-<rust-target-triple>[.exe]` (`release.yml:70-76`). Notes are generated by `softprops/action-gh-release@v2` with `generate_release_notes: true` and `fail_on_unmatched_files: true`.
- **Version bump** is manual: edit `Cargo.toml`, regenerate `Cargo.lock`, commit `chore: bump version to X`, tag `vX`, push (`docs/history/release-v0.5.2/reports/release-v0.5.2-1.md`). The binary reads its version only from `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")` (`cli.rs:191`).
- **Checksums and signing:** the release publishes no checksum file and does no signing. `update` relies on the `sha256:` digest GitHub computes for each asset (`update.rs:49-50`).

### Install scripts
**`install.sh`** (90 lines, POSIX `sh`, `set -eu`):
- **Platform detection** (`:18-31`): `uname -s`/`-m` is mapped to the target triple. Linux is always `unknown-linux-musl`. Unsupported systems get the `cargo install` command in the error.
- **Install directory** (`:33-40`): the first writable of `/usr/local/bin` → `~/.local/bin` → `~/.mdview/bin`. Override with `MDVIEW_INSTALL_DIR`.
- **Pinned version:** `MDVIEW_VERSION` (default `latest`). It uses the `releases/latest/download/<asset>` URL, so there is no API call and no rate limit.
- **Safe replacement while running** (`:56-65`):
  ```sh
  # Download beside the target, then rename over it: writing straight into the
  # binary fails with "Text file busy" while an `mdview serve` daemon runs from it
  TMP="$DIR/.$BIN.download.$$"; trap 'rm -f "$TMP"' EXIT
  HTTP_CODE="$(curl -sSL -w '%{http_code}' -o "$TMP" "$URL")" || true
  ```
- **Fallback on HTTP status:**
  - 200 → install the binary.
  - 404 → `cargo install --git … --root "${DIR%/bin}"`.
  - anything else → a hard error. A network failure never silently falls through to a source build.
- **PATH:** it only prints a hint when the directory is missing (`:76-79`) and never edits shell rc files.
- **Ending:** it runs `"$DIR/$BIN" --version` and prints the next steps (`doctor --fix`, `doctor --fix --mcp`, `serve`).
- **Re-running** is safe (it says so in the header).

**`install.ps1`** does the same on Windows:
- It accepts only AMD64 (checking `PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432` for 32-bit PowerShell) and installs to `%USERPROFILE%\.mdview\bin`.
- To replace a running exe it moves the current one to `.old` first, then moves the new one in (`:55-62`).
- It prints the `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', …, 'User')` line but does not run it.

**Neither script verifies checksums, and neither has an uninstall mode.** Uninstall lives in the binary.

### Self-update (`crates/mdview/src/update.rs`)
- **Flags:** `mdview update [--check] [--version vX] [--force]`. Setting `GITHUB_TOKEN` lifts the anonymous API rate limit (`:119-124`).
- **The update repo comes from package metadata**, so it can't drift: `env!("CARGO_PKG_REPOSITORY")` (`:17-21`).
- **Asset name** is chosen by `cfg!` and matches the release naming (`:25-37`). A test guards the match.
- **Download checks:**
  - exact byte size, then the GitHub `sha256:` digest (`verify_download`, `:70-93`);
  - a **smoke test** (`:224-258`): the staged binary must answer `--version` with exactly the target version within 30 s. This catches truncated, wrong-platform and wrong-tag downloads.
- **Staging and swap:**
  - The new file is written next to the real binary (symlinks resolved, `:149-152`), so the rename stays on one filesystem.
  - Unix: an atomic `rename`.
  - Windows: rename the running exe to `.old-<pid>`, move the new one in, and roll back on failure (`:263-292`). Every start deletes parked `.old*` files (`main.rs:28` → `cleanup_parked_binary`).
- **Downgrade policy** is a pure, tested function (`should_install`, `:311-322`). Only an explicit `--version` pin can downgrade; `--force` only reinstalls the same version.
- **After the swap:**
  - It runs the **new** binary by path, `doctor --after-update` (`:407-412`), so the templates compiled into the new version get installed.
  - It then runs `restart` if a daemon is up.
- **Under sudo** (`running_under_sudo`: euid 0 plus `SUDO_UID`), it skips the daemon and skill steps because they belong to the user, and prints what to run as yourself.
- **Daemon version checks:** the daemon is auto-replaced when it is older (`runtime.rs:209-263`, `needs_restart` compares schema first, then semver, and never downgrades). `spawn_daemon_detached` strips Linux's `" (deleted)"` suffix from `current_exe` after a swap (`runtime.rs:143-149`).
- **MCP is a thin proxy** that shells out to `mdview view-file` on every call, so connected MCP clients pick up a new binary without reconnecting.

### Config (`crates/mdview-core/src/config.rs`)
- **One data directory, `~/.mdview/`** (not XDG). It holds `config.toml`, `registry-v4.db` and `daemon.lock`.
- Every struct is `#[serde(default)]`. A missing file becomes the defaults, and a **corrupt file also becomes the defaults** with only a `tracing::warn` (`:165-173`).
- **Writes are atomic** (`write_atomic`, `:216-235`): a temp file in the same directory, then rename. It **keeps the existing file's permissions** (for example a 0600 `~/.claude.json`). The same helper is reused for every edit to third-party configs.
- **Discoverable optional keys:** `with_hostname_hint` adds a commented `# hostname = "my-host.local"` line after `host =`.
- **Renamed keys** are handled with `#[serde(alias = "host_name")]`.
- **Schema migration by generation** (`registry_db_path`, `:143`): the database file name carries the schema version (`registry-v4.db`), so older binaries and daemons keep working on their own file. `doctor --fix` deletes the legacy files.
- **Editing:** `mdview config edit` opens `$VISUAL`, then `$EDITOR`, then `vi`/`notepad`, and re-validates the TOML after saving. There is also a web Settings page.
- **Environment variables:** effectively none override config. The only ones are `RUST_LOG`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `VISUAL`/`EDITOR`, `WSL_DISTRO_NAME` and the installer's `MDVIEW_*`.

### Doctor (`crates/mdview/src/doctor.rs`)
- **Flags:** `mdview doctor [--fix] [--dry-run] [--json] [--mcp]`, plus a hidden `--after-update`.
- **Statuses** (`:9-39`): `OK ✓ / FIXED + / MANUAL ! / WARN ~ / SKIP –`. `--json` prints `{checks:[{check,status,detail}]}`.
- **Checks:**
  - binary on PATH;
  - config present;
  - daemon running, **asking the live process for its version** rather than trusting the lock file (`:145-199`);
  - index schema, read from SQLite `PRAGMA user_version` through a **read-only** connection so a diagnosis never creates or modifies the database (`:205-221`);
  - the Claude permission `Bash(mdview open:*)`;
  - MCP registration for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and Claude Desktop;
  - the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md instruction block;
  - the global skill.
- **It only writes config for tools that are actually installed** (`claude_present`/`codex_present`/`antigravity_present`, `:488-497`). Anything else is `SKIP`.

### Agent integration
- **Managed marker block.** `<!-- mdview:START -->…<!-- mdview:END -->` is inserted or replaced in `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` (`:847-902`).
  - It writes **through symlinks** (`CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md`) and leaves the user's content around the block alone.
  - It counts as in sync only when the block text matches exactly.
  - The text comes from `include_str!("docs/mdview-agents-template.md")`, using only what follows the `---` preamble. `.gitattributes` forces LF on these templates.
- **Skill.** The global `~/.claude/skills/mdview/SKILL.md` is a whole-file match against the embedded `docs/mdview-skill-template.md`. `after_update` refreshes it only if it already exists (`:1029-1049`).
- **MCP registration:**
  - JSON `mcpServers.mdview = {command: <current_exe>, args:["mcp"]}`, with a `.bak` copy first.
  - Codex TOML is edited with `toml_edit`, so comments survive. It uses an explicit `[mcp_servers.mdview]` table to avoid duplicate-key clashes with inline tables (`:596-610`), and a malformed file is left unchanged.
- **WSL to Claude Desktop on Windows** (`:701-781`): it detects WSL (`WSL_DISTRO_NAME` or `/proc/version`), searches `/mnt/c/Users/*/AppData/Roaming/Claude`, and registers `wsl.exe -d <distro> -e <exe> mcp`.
- **MCP is opt-in** (`--mcp`). The CLI plus the instruction block is the main route, and MCP is meant for clients without a shell.

### Uninstall (`crates/mdview/src/uninstall.rs`)
- **Flags:** `mdview uninstall [--purge] [-y] [--dry-run]` (alias `remove`).
- **Plan, then apply** (`:530-553`, `run` at `:959-1037`): it builds a list of `Step{what, irreversible, apply}`, prints it and asks for confirmation. With no TTY it refuses unless `--yes` is given.
- **Each step reverses one thing `doctor --fix` creates.** It stops the daemon, removes the permission and the MCP entries (JSON and TOML), deletes the skill and its directory if empty, strips the managed block, and deletes a file that held only the block (unless the file is symlinked).
- **Config edits are safe:** it re-reads each config at apply time, because Claude Code rewrites `~/.claude.json` often (`:614-629`), and makes a timestamped `.mdview-<secs>.bak` first.
- **Irreversible steps** (binary, data directory) are skipped once any earlier step fails, so the user can fix the cause and re-run.
- **Symlinks:** it also removes `mdview` symlinks on PATH that point to the binary.
- **Windows:** the running exe can't be deleted, so it is handed to a detached `cmd` (`ping -n 3 … & del …`) that runs after the process exits (`:906-941`). It strips `\\?\` prefixes and leaves paths containing `%` or `"` to the user.
- **Scope:** it refuses to run under sudo. Other registered projects that still have the block are **listed, not edited**. Without `--purge` the data directory is kept.

### Docs / UX
- **README:** a two-line install section, then upgrade and uninstall pointers, a `cargo install` fallback, and a "Use it with your agent" section that explains each of the three things `doctor --fix` writes.
- **`docs/usage.md`** covers Install, Upgrading, Uninstalling, Settings and "Where things live" (§1, §5, §7).
- **Installers end with explicit "Next:" commands.**
- **Error messages include the fix**, for example `sudo mdview update`, `sudo rm <path>`, or `cargo install … --force` for platforms with no binary.

## 3. Notable good ideas
1. **Asset name = Rust target triple, served at `releases/latest/download/<name>`.** Installer, updater and workflow share one naming rule with no JSON parsing, and a unit test ties the updater to it.
2. **Fall back to `cargo install` only on a 404, and fail hard on any other HTTP error.** Missing platforms still work, and network problems are never hidden.
3. **Download beside the target, then rename.** This avoids "Text file busy" and lets a running daemon keep its old inode. On Windows, rename the running exe aside and clean `.old-<pid>` files on the next start.
4. **Smoke-test the new binary (`--version` must equal the target) before swapping.** It is a cheap check against truncated, wrong-arch or mislabeled downloads.
5. **After a swap, run follow-up steps through the new binary by path.** The running process holds the old embedded templates.
6. **Keep the downgrade policy in a pure, tested function.** Only an explicit pin downgrades, and `--force` never does.
7. **Take the update repo from `CARGO_PKG_REPOSITORY`.** There is one source of truth, so a fork updates from itself.
8. **Make a sudo-aware updater and uninstaller.** They never modify a user's daemon or home directory while running as root.
9. **Use an atomic write that keeps file permissions** for every config you touch, including third-party ones. It won't widen access on a 0600 secret.
10. **Use managed `START/END` marker blocks for shared instruction files.** Upsert is idempotent and reversible, writes go through symlinks, and the templates are embedded with `include_str!` plus an LF `.gitattributes` rule.
11. **Detect a tool before writing its config** (Status `SKIP`), so nothing gets installed for tools that aren't there.
12. **Edit TOML with `toml_edit` and leave malformed files untouched.** User comments survive.
13. **Make uninstall the exact inverse of doctor, as plan → confirm → apply.** It re-reads files at apply time, makes timestamped backups, skips irreversible steps after a failure, and has `--dry-run`, `--purge` and `--yes`.

## 3. Notable good ideas
1. **Asset name = Rust target triple, served at `releases/latest/download/<name>`.** Installer, updater and workflow share one naming rule with no JSON parsing, and a unit test ties the updater to it.
2. **Fall back to `cargo install` only on a 404, and fail hard on any other HTTP error.** Missing platforms still work, and network problems are never hidden.
3. **Download beside the target, then rename.** This avoids "Text file busy" and lets a running daemon keep its old inode. On Windows, rename the running exe aside and clean `.old-<pid>` files on the next start.
4. **Smoke-test the new binary (`--version` must equal the target) before swapping.** It is a cheap check against truncated, wrong-arch or mislabeled downloads.
5. **After a swap, run follow-up steps through the new binary by path.** The running process holds the old embedded templates.
6. **Keep the downgrade policy in a pure, tested function.** Only an explicit pin downgrades, and `--force` never does.
7. **Take the update repo from `CARGO_PKG_REPOSITORY`.** There is one source of truth, so a fork updates from itself.
8. **Make a sudo-aware updater and uninstaller.** They never modify a user's daemon or home directory while running as root.
9. **Use an atomic write that keeps file permissions** for every config you touch, including third-party ones. It won't widen access on a 0600 secret.
10. **Use managed `START/END` marker blocks for shared instruction files.** Upsert is idempotent and reversible, writes go through symlinks, and the templates are embedded with `include_str!` plus an LF `.gitattributes` rule.
11. **Detect a tool before writing its config** (Status `SKIP`), so nothing gets installed for tools that aren't there.
12. **Edit TOML with `toml_edit` and leave malformed files untouched.** User comments survive.
13. **Make uninstall the exact inverse of doctor, as plan → confirm → apply.** It re-reads files at apply time, makes timestamped backups, skips irreversible steps after a failure, and has `--dry-run`, `--purge` and `--yes`.
14. **Version the database by file name (`registry-v4.db`).** Old and new binaries coexist safely during upgrades, and doctor cleans up the legacy files.
15. **Auto-replace a stale daemon by asking the live process its version.** An upgraded binary never talks to an older server.
16. **Make the MCP server a thin per-call proxy to the CLI.** Updates apply without clients reconnecting.
17. **Build static musl binaries for Linux.** One binary runs on every distro.
18. **Commit pre-built JS bundles and embed them.** Building the Rust binary never needs Node.

## 4. Gaps / weaknesses
- **The install scripts verify nothing.** There is no sha256 check, although `update` has one. The release has no `SHA256SUMS` file, no signature (minisign, cosign) and no GitHub attestation or SBOM. GitHub's asset `digest` only proves the download arrived intact; it says nothing about where the binary came from.
- **The release isn't gated on CI.** Nothing checks that the tag matches the `Cargo.toml` version (the update smoke test would only catch a mismatch later). The version bump is manual with no script (`cargo-release`, `just release`). There is no CHANGELOG.
- **Assets are bare binaries.** No archive, no LICENSE, and no completions or man page alongside them.
- **Platform coverage is thin.** No Intel macOS, Windows arm64, or Linux armv7 prebuilts. `install.ps1` has no arm64 path.

- **`install.sh` requires `curl`** (no `wget` fallback) and never updates PATH itself.
- **No shell completions** (no `clap_complete`) and no man pages.
- **Config gaps:**
  - It isn't XDG or OS-native, and there's no `MDVIEW_HOME`/`MDVIEW_CONFIG` override.
  - No environment variable can override a config key, so precedence is just CLI flags (`serve --host/--port`) over the file over defaults.

  - Intel Macs are deliberately unsupported (`install.sh:98`).
- **Embedded web UI:**
  - `npm ci && npm run bundle` runs before `cargo build`. Vite outputs to `../static` (`web/vite.config.ts:7`).
  - `#[derive(RustEmbed)] #[folder = "static/"]` with `debug-embed` (`src/web/mod.rs:28`).
  - `build.rs:15` runs `create_dir_all("static")` so a fresh checkout still compiles.
  - An on-disk `static_dir/index.html` overrides the embedded copy; doctor reports which one is in use.
- **Version injection** (`build.rs:17-22`):
  - Produces `0.1.22 (abc123-dirty, 2026-…T…+07:00)` and passes it as `HERDR_GO_FINGERPRINT`, which becomes `herdr_go::VERSION` (`src/lib.rs:24`).
  - It deliberately emits no `rerun-if` lines, so the dirty flag and timestamp never go stale.
  - It falls back to `nogit` when git is unavailable.
- **Release profile:** `strip = true`, `lto = "thin"`.
- **Archive contents:** binary, `config.example.json`, `install.sh`, README, the matching service file (plist or systemd unit), and the docs (`release.yml:75-93`).
- **Checksums:**
  - Each job uploads its archive as a workflow artifact.
  - A `checksums` job (`needs: [build, release-windows]`) merges them and runs `scripts/generate-checksums.sh dist > checksums.txt`. The output goes outside the scanned folder so the file never hashes itself.
  - If any build fails, no checksums are published, so updates fail closed.
- **Tests against the published assets:**
  - `windows-install-smoke.ps1`: install.ps1, then Scheduled Task, crash-restart, uninstall.
  - `macos-install-smoke.sh`: the same flow with a LaunchAgent.
  - `update-smoke.sh`: installs the *previous* tag, resolved dynamically (`release.yml:283-291`), runs `herdr-go update`, and checks that the `/api/health` version changed.
  - Windows CI also downloads a hash-pinned upstream herdr binary to test against the real runtime (`release.yml:148-161`).
- **Version discipline** (`scripts/check-version.sh`, `.githooks/pre-commit`):
  - **pre-commit:** blocks a commit that changes `src/`, `web/src/`, `scripts/` or `Cargo.toml` without a version bump. It also enforces that versions only go up (via `sort -V`) and that `herdr-plugin.toml` matches. Bypass with `SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1`.
  - **`ci`:** compares against the latest tag.
  - **`drift`:** on `main` only, a non-failing note when the version is ahead of the last release ("release may be overdue").
- **Dev deploy:** `dev-deploy.sh` builds and installs a separate `herdr-go-dev.service` from the template `packaging/herdr-go-dev.service`, filling `@REPO@`, `@ENVFILE@` and the other placeholders with `sed`. It stops the conflicting production and legacy units. `--logs` tails the journal.

### Install
- **install.sh** (Linux and macOS, 243 lines):
  - Only one flag, `--uninstall`.
  - `PREFIX` (default `~/.local`) puts the binary in `$PREFIX/bin`.
  - `HERDR_GO_VERSION` pins a tag; the default is `latest` via `releases/latest/download/...`.
  - Downloads use `curl -fSL --proto '=https'` into a `mktemp -d` folder cleaned by `trap`, and check the archive layout.
  - Paths are the OS-native ones and are commented "MUST match `src/config/mod.rs`": XDG on Linux, a single `~/Library/Application Support/herdr-go` on macOS.
  - Preflight checks before anything is touched (`:106-116`): `launchctl` is present, or `systemctl --user show-environment` works.
  - `migrate_dir` moves legacy `herdr-gateway` folders and fails closed if both old and new exist (`:118-130`).
  - The default config comes from the binary itself: `herdr-go --internal-print-default-config > config.json`, only if no config exists (`:149-153`).
  - The token is written to `herdr-go.env` with `umask 077` and `chmod 600` from `openssl rand -hex 24`, falling back to `/dev/urandom`. It is printed only on first creation.
  - **Idempotent:** on macOS it runs `bootout` before `bootstrap`, falling back to `load -w`. On Linux it disables conflicting legacy and dev units.
- **install.ps1** (199 lines):
  - `-Uninstall`; no elevation needed.
  - Installs to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\herdr-go\bin`, with config in `%APPDATA%\herdr-go`.
  - Registers a per-user `AtLogOn` Scheduled Task with `RunLevel Limited`, `-RestartCount 3 -RestartInterval 1min`. Comments note the 1-minute minimum, versus systemd's 3 seconds.
  - **Notable choice:** the installer never writes the token file (`install.ps1:20-28`). The binary creates it with an owner-only access list (DACL, set through Win32 calls), because a file written by PowerShell would inherit ACL entries that the binary's own check then rejects. The installer polls for the file for up to 10 seconds and prints the token once.
- **Neither installer** verifies `checksums.txt` or adds the binary folder to PATH.

### Self-update (`src/update/`)
- **Flow:** check the GitHub API for `releases/latest` → compare the version parsed from the start of the fingerprint (`update/mod.rs:51`, a small hand-written `SemVer`) → pick the asset name in `asset.rs`, which mirrors install.sh's mapping → download the asset and `checksums.txt` → fail closed if the checksum file is missing, the entry is missing, or the hash doesn't match (`github.rs` `FetchError`).
- **Rollout** (`rollout.rs:67-106`):
  1. Stop the service.
  2. Back up the binary to `<exe>.bak-<nanos>`, then write a staged file and rename it into place (atomic swap, `swap.rs:45-93`).
  3. Run the **new** binary as a separate process with `--internal-merge-config <path>`, so new defaults come from the new version's own compiled defaults.
  4. Start the service.
  5. Poll `127.0.0.1:<port>/api/health` 10 times, 1 second apart.
  6. If health never comes up, restore both the binary and the config and start again.
- **Config merge** (`config/merge.rs`): only adds missing keys, never overwrites user values, keeps orphaned keys, backs up first, and validates through `Config::load_str` before writing.

### Config
- **Format:** JSON with `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`.
- **Validation:** `load_str` collects every error before reporting.
- **No secrets in config:** there is deliberately no token field.
- **Paths:**
  - Linux: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/herdr-go`, with data in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/herdr-go`.
  - macOS: Application Support.
  - Windows: Known Folders `RoamingAppData` and `LocalAppData`.
- **Zero-config:** running with no flags auto-creates a default whose `allowed_roots` is `~/projects` if it exists, otherwise `~`.
- **Secret precedence** (`config/mod.rs:926`): environment variable `HERDR_GO_WEB_SECRET`, then `herdr-go.env`, which must pass `validate_token_protection` (mode `&0o077==0` and owner == euid, or an owner-only DACL), then a newly generated token written with `create_new` and mode 600.
- **Other environment variables:** `HERDR_GO_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `HERDR_GO_TELEGRAM_TOKEN`, `HERDR_GO_HERDR_BINARY`, `RUST_LOG`.
- **CLI:** `-c/--config`, `-b/--bind` (an override that prints a security notice when not loopback), `--demo` (in-memory fake herdr).
- **Legacy migration** (`migrate_legacy_state`) only runs on a normal default-config startup. It is skipped for doctor, demo and explicit `--config` runs (`main.rs:52`, which has a mode-matrix test).

### Doctor (`src/doctor/`)
- **Checks:** herdr binary, config, herdr endpoint, herdr reachable (including a protocol-number match), web token, allowed roots, agent presets, web UI source (embedded or on disk), bind address.
- **Each check** is ok, fail, info or skipped, and carries `critical` and `fix` hints.
- **Phases** (`doctor/mod.rs:26`):
  1. Diagnose.
  2. At a terminal, offer guided fixes.
  3. Re-run everything, so the exit code reflects the state after fixes.
  4. An optional settings editor.
- **Read-only mode:** `--check`, or any run without a terminal. The exit code is 0 only if every critical check passes.

### Service control
`herdr-go service start|stop|restart|status` passes straight through to `systemctl --user`, `launchctl` (`gui/<uid>`) or PowerShell Scheduled Task commands (`checks.rs:388-471`). By design it has no retry logic of its own.
- **Unit hardening:** `NoNewPrivileges`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ReadWritePaths=$DATA_DIR $CONFIG_DIR`, `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=3`.
- **Linger:** `loginctl enable-linger` keeps the service running after logout.
- **macOS plist:** `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false`, `ThrottleInterval=3`. It contains no secrets, because the binary reads its own `.env` file.

### Uninstall
Removes only the service registration and the binary. Config, data and the token are always kept, and the script prints a line saying so. Manual `rm -rf` steps are in `docs/installation.md:64-77`.

### Plugin manifest (`herdr-plugin.toml`)
A "thin launcher" only:
- `id = "herdr.herdr-go"`, `min_herdr_version = "0.7.3"`, three platforms.
- Two **read-only** actions: `herdr-go service status` and `herdr-go url`.
- Start, stop and restart are left out deliberately, because herdr-go supervises herdr and should not be controllable from herdr's UI.
- No `[[build]]` step; the binaries come from releases.

### Docs, UX and AI agents
- README gives the one-line installs. `docs/installation.md` covers service management, upgrade, uninstall, login token retrieval and rotation, and a "where things live" table.
- `docs/specs/*.md` (`self-update`, `doctor`, `installation`, `service-lifecycle`) plus `docs/history/<feature>/CONTEXT.md` hold numbered decisions (D1…), which code comments cite.
- `tests/rename_contract.sh` is a static contract test. It checks installer/release asset-name agreement, that the docs packaged in releases exist, README links, systemd hardening, and that retired names are gone.
- AI integration: `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`, plus the same `herdr-orchestrating` skill in both `.claude/skills/` and `.agents/skills/`, for a dispatch/merge agent loop.

## 3. Ideas worth copying
1. **Let the binary generate its own default config** (`--internal-print-default-config`), so installers, `ensure_config` and the update merge share one source and don't drift.
2. **Merge config by running the new binary as a child process** (`--internal-merge-config`) after the swap, so new defaults come from the new version rather than the old running one.
3. **Self-update as verify → atomic swap → health check → automatic rollback of binary and config**, which avoids bricking a service on a bad release.
4. **Publish one `checksums.txt` only after every build job succeeds**, so clients never trust a partial set.
5. **Run tests after publishing against the real end-user path**: curl-install, service, crash-restart, uninstall, and update-from-previous-tag, with the previous tag resolved dynamically so the test can't go stale.
6. **Put a version fingerprint (semver + sha + dirty + timestamp) in the binary and expose it on `/api/health`**, which lets update tests prove the version actually changed.
7. **Use a pre-commit hook that requires a version bump on code changes, plus a CI check that versions only go up, plus a non-failing drift notice**, so versions stay honest and releases don't silently fall behind.
8. **Keep secrets out of service files**: the binary loads its own mode-600 / owner-only `.env` file and refuses to start if its permissions are too loose.
9. **Uninstall should never delete user config, data or tokens**, and should say so.
10. **Make installers safe to re-run** (bootout or unregister before registering) and **check the service manager is reachable before touching anything**.
11. **Use static musl Linux builds**, so the binary runs on any distro.
12. **Doctor has two modes:** read-only `--check` for scripts and CI, guided fixes at a terminal, and a re-run so the exit code reflects the state after fixes.
13. **`build.rs` creates the embed folder**, so a fresh checkout compiles without npm.
14. **Use a static "contract" test script** that cross-checks asset names, paths and doc links across workflows, installers and docs.
15. **Pin CI runner images and hash-pin third-party binaries** downloaded during CI.
16. **Keep a plugin/marketplace manifest as a thin, read-only launcher** for the existing CLI.

## 4. Gaps and weaknesses
- **Update installs the archive as the binary.** `download_and_verify` returns the bytes of `herdr-go-<target>.tar.gz` or `.zip`, and `perform_update` writes them over the executable without extracting (`github.rs:142-158`, `rollout.rs:77`). There is no tar or zip dependency in `Cargo.toml`. The health check should then fail and roll back every time, so I expect `update-smoke` to fail. Inferred from the code; not run.
- **Windows update:** replacing a running `.exe` is a known unsupported path (`rollout.rs:17-21`).
- **Installers don't verify checksums.** install.sh and install.ps1 never fetch `checksums.txt`. There is no signing, SBOM or build provenance either.
- **Installer and binary versions can mismatch.** Installers run from raw `main` while the binary may be a pinned `HERDR_GO_VERSION` tag.
- **Broken uninstall URL on macOS.** install.sh prints `releases/latest/download/install.sh` (`:209`), but `install.sh` is only inside the tarball, not published as a separate release file, so that URL should 404. `docs/installation.md` gives the raw `main` URL instead.
- **No PATH handling.** Nothing checks or adds `~/.local/bin` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\herdr-go\bin` to PATH, yet the plugin actions and `herdr-go service` depend on PATH.
- **Inconsistent first-run behavior.** Linux enables the service but doesn't start it; macOS and Windows start it. Linux generates the token in the installer, Windows in the binary.
- **Three copies of the default config.** `config.example.json` (`herdr_session: "gateway"`, `CHANGE_ME` root) has drifted from `default_config_json` (`"default"`). It is a `format!` with `{root:?}` (Rust debug formatting), which can produce invalid JSON for non-ASCII paths.
- **Possible update race.** `check_for_update` and `download_and_verify` each fetch `releases/latest` separately, so a release published in between could be installed without its version check.
- **Leftover files.** Update backups `*.bak-<nanos>` pile up with no cleanup. Health checks only target loopback.
- **Silent empty UI.** An empty `static/` still builds, so a release shipped without running the web bundle would have no UI and nothing would fail.
- **Contract test and hooks not wired up.** `tests/rename_contract.sh` isn't run in CI. The `.githooks` folder is never activated (`core.hooksPath` is not set up or documented).
- **Release and test ordering.** Assets are published before the smoke tests run, with no draft-then-promote step. A failing test leaves a bad release live.
- **Not supported:** shell completions, Intel macOS builds, Windows ARM, glibc builds, a package-manager channel.

The product ships a tiny bootstrap binary, `fgctl`. `fgctl` downloads a release tree, checks its digest and activates it for one project. The activated release then wires itself into the project and coding agents through `setup` and `doctor`.

# Forgent (fgOS) packaging and distribution practices

## 1. Stack and distribution channels

- **Stack.**
  - A Rust Cargo workspace with about 28 crates. Two binaries: `apps/fgctl` (installer and runtime manager) and `apps/fgos` (the host).
  - A Node ESM package, `forgent` 0.2.0 (`package.json`, `"private": true`). Its bins are `fgos` → `bin/fgos.mjs` and `fgos-runner`.
  - A napi native addon (`fgos_node_addon`) that the Node code loads.
- **Channels:**
  1. **Primary.** GitHub Releases assets: `fgctl-<tag>-<triple>.tar.gz`, `fgos-<tag>-<triple>.tar.gz`, `SHA256SUMS`, `install.sh`, `install.ps1`. You install with `curl … | sh` or `irm … | iex`, then run `fgctl init` inside each project.
  2. **Legacy.** `npm install -g github:vantt/forgent#v0.1.0`. It is not on the npm registry, and the README marks it as a compatibility channel (`README.md:102-116`).
  3. **Dev checkout.** Source `scripts/fgos-shell-integration.sh` to get `fgos` shell functions.
  4. **Claude Code plugin marketplace.** `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` lists `plugins/fgOS` and `plugins/dogfood-fixture`.
- **Targets.** Only `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` (glibc 2.35 or newer) and `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. macOS and ARM are not supported.

## 2. Area by area

### Build and release
- **Three-step pipeline.**
  - `release.yml` runs on a `v*` tag. Its `check-version` job fails if the tag's base version differs from `package.json` (`release.yml:18-27`). Pre-release is inferred from a `-` in the tag (`:91-93`).
  - `release-assets.yml` is a reusable `workflow_call` that builds and proves the assets but never publishes. `release-assets-check.yml` runs it on every push and PR to `main`, so release packaging is tested before anyone tags.
- **Single packaging definition.** `scripts/package-release-assets.mjs:15-17` says it is "the one place the asset names, the archive layout and the checksum file are defined, so a release, the CI consumer proof and a local dry run can never package differently."
- **Release tree with a manifest.** `scripts/build-rust-distribution.mjs` builds `bin/fgos`, a `bin/fgos-runner` shim (sh and `.cmd`), `libexec/legacy-node/` and `manifest.json`.
  - The manifest lists every file with digest, mode and class (`immutable-entry`, `immutable-runtime`, `metadata` …), plus `requires.node`, the target and a content-addressed `artifactDigest`.
  - The digest is a SHA-256 of a sorted-key (JCS) JSON manifest with the digest field left out (`:37-49`, `:438-473`). The release's identity is that digest, not its version string.
- **Hardening in the release job:**
  - `cargo deny check advisories bans sources` (`release-assets.yml:22-29`).
  - Linux builds on `ubuntu-22.04`, and `scripts/check-glibc-ceiling.sh` runs `objdump -T` to fail any binary that needs a glibc newer than `GLIBC_CEILING` (default 2.35).
  - Reproducibility check: an `independent-addon` job rebuilds the addon on a clean machine without cache, and `compare-addon` runs `cmp` on the two digests (`:125-173`). Windows uses `/Brepro` for a deterministic linker.
  - **External consumer proof.** `scripts/ci-external-consumer.sh --assets dist` (plus `.ps1` under PowerShell 5.1 and 7) installs from the built assets outside the checkout before anything is uploaded.
  - In the publish job, `install.sh` and `install.ps1` must be byte-identical across target builds (`release.yml:55-67`). The job merges SHA256SUMS, runs `sha256sum --check`, and asserts that every triple × kind asset exists.
- **Release prep.** `npm run release:check` / `release:prepare` (`scripts/prepare-release.mjs`):
  - parses semver plus pre-release;
  - refuses a dirty tree;
  - updates `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, three Cargo manifests and three Cargo lockfiles, leaving vendored third-party crates alone (`:75-110`);
  - moves `## [Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` under a dated tag heading;
  - prints the `git add` / `commit` / `tag` commands rather than running them.

### Install (`install.sh`, 206 lines, POSIX sh)
- Refuses to run as root unless `FGCTL_ALLOW_ROOT=1` (`:5-8`). Points Windows-shell users to `install.ps1` (`:22-25`).
- **Env vars:**
  - `FGCTL_TARGET`
  - `FGCTL_VERSION`: needed for pre-releases, because GitHub's "latest" never points at one.
  - `FGCTL_ASSET_BASE_URL`: mirror or air-gapped installs.
  - `FGCTL_INSTALL_DIR`: default `~/.local/bin`.
- **Bounded network calls.** curl gets `--max-time 120`. wget gets a wall-clock backstop through `timeout 130`, because wget's `--timeout` is only an idle timeout (comment at `:41-55`).
- Resolves "latest" by following the `/releases/latest` redirect (`curl -w '%{url_effective}'`), so it never calls the GitHub API and is not rate-limited (`:80-92`).
- **Checksum matched by exact filename,** never by substring:
  ```sh
  awk -v f="$TARBALL" '{ n = $2; sub(/^\*/, "", n); if (n == f) { print; exit } }' SHA256SUMS
  ```
  It falls back from `sha256sum` to `shasum -a 256` (`:129-153`).
- Refuses a symlinked `fgctl` in the tarball (`:163-177`). The install is atomic: copy to `.fgctl.$$.tmp`, `chmod 755`, then `mv -f` (`:182-185`). A `trap` cleans up on EXIT, INT and TERM.
- **PATH advice only.** It never edits rc files; it prints the `export` line (`:187-201`). It ends with a next step: `fgctl init`.
- `scripts/install.ps1` mirrors this on Windows: `Get-FileHash`, System32 `tar.exe` (Git-for-Windows tar misreads `C:`), install to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\fgos\bin`, and PATH left unchanged with the `SetEnvironmentVariable` command printed instead.

### Project activation, update and rollback (`fgctl`, `packages/distribution/rust`)
- **Subcommands.** `fgctl stage|status [--json]|init|upgrade|repair|verify` (`apps/fgctl/src/main.rs:9-22`).
- **Source precedence** is printed in the usage text and implemented in `fetch.rs:156-174`: `--from <path|URL>` > `FGCTL_FROM` > `FGCTL_VERSION=<tag>` > the project's committed pin > latest. URL sources need a `SHA256SUMS` file next to them. Target detection matches `install.sh` (`detect_target_for`, which tests can drive for any OS).
- **Machine release store,** content-addressed:
  - Location: `${FGOS_STATE_ROOT}` or `${FGOS_STATE_HOME:-${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/fgos}`, holding `releases/<digest>/`, `quarantine/` and `installs/<activation_id>.json` transaction records (`store.rs:66-71`, `:259-277`).
  - A machine-wide `locks/install.lock` is a kernel lock, tried once without waiting, and is freed automatically if the holder dies (`store.rs:25-63`).
- **Committed project pin** `.fgos/distribution.json`:
  ```json
  {"schemaVersion":1,"projectRuntime":{"policy":"exact-digest","artifactDigest":"sha256:…","releaseVersion":null,"channel":null,"allowPrerelease":false}}
  ```
  A downloaded release writes its tag here, so a teammate who runs a plain `fgctl init` gets the same verified bytes (README `:89-91`).
- **Per-workspace activation** in `.fgos/installation/`, which is gitignored (`.gitignore:43`):
  - `root.json`
  - `activation.json`: status, `artifactDigest`, `releasePath`, `previousArtifactDigest`, `pinSnapshot`, `activatedBy {tool, version}`
  - stable shims in `bin/fgos` and `bin/fgos.cmd`

  `activation.json` is written as a temp file plus `fsync`, then renamed, then the directory is `fsync`ed (`init.rs:518-553`).
- **Stable shim.** The `sh` shim (`shim.rs:27-…`) reads `activation.json` with shell builtins only, because it runs on every agent hook call. It namespaces its variables as `_fgos_*`, refuses unless `status == ready`, and points you to `fgctl repair`.
- **After activation** `run_tail` runs `fgos init`, then `doctor --fix`, then `doctor`. On failure it marks the transaction `ready-degraded` (`init.rs:555-600`).
- **Lifecycle commands:**
  - `upgrade` deliberately ignores the pin and goes to latest unless told otherwise (`init.rs:1343-1346`).
  - `repair` rolls back to `previousArtifactDigest`.
  - `verify` re-hashes the active release against its manifest and quarantines it on mismatch. A quarantined activation is never skipped as "already done", and the rollback chain skips past it (`init.rs:999-1006`).
- **Extraction safety.** `extract.rs:18-25` rejects absolute, `..`, drive-letter, symlink, hardlink and device entries.

### Config
- **Layers.** Project `.fgos/config.yaml` (tracked) over global `~/.fgos/config.yaml` (mode 0600) over a bundled **standard** (`core/config-standard/*.yaml`). Secrets go in `~/.fgos/private/` (0700): `accounts.yaml` and `gateway-token`.
- Precedence is project > global > detected > standard (`docs/platform/config/spec.md:52-66`).
- **Files hold only differences.** A value equal to the standard is flagged as `config-redundant-value`. Every changed key carries `# @fgos:why` and `# @fgos:doc` comments (see `.fgos/config.yaml`).
- **Project file not trusted for machine keys.** Schema annotations `x-fgos-scope: global-only|project-only` and `x-fgos-sensitivity` refuse those keys in the wrong file by name (`spec.md:70-73`).
- **Verbs.** `fgos config show|explain|standard|check|set --reason|unset|patch|migrate|refresh-docs`. Merging and validation live in Rust only, and Node goes through a facade.

### Doctor and setup
- **`fgos doctor`** (`bin/fgos.mjs:4171-4190`):
  - Read-only by default. `--fix` runs registered fixes, then re-checks. `--strict` exits 1 on any failure; otherwise it always exits 0. `--pretty` prints human-readable output; JSON is the default.
  - It resolves the *main* checkout even when run from a linked worktree.

## 3. Notable good ideas worth copying

1. **Tiny bootstrap binary plus a per-project pinned runtime.** The installer stays small and rarely changes, while each repo pins its exact runtime, so teammates and CI get identical bits.
2. **Content-addressed releases (digest of a canonical manifest) with the pin committed to git.** Identity can't be faked by renaming a version, and it makes `verify`, quarantine and rollback straightforward.
3. **The reusable "build assets" workflow runs on every PR, and only the tag workflow publishes.** Packaging breakage is caught before release day.
4. **One packaging script for local, CI and release builds.** The three can't drift apart.
5. **An external-consumer proof installs from the built assets outside the checkout in CI** (sh, PowerShell 5.1 and 7). It tests what users actually run.
6. **A glibc ceiling check plus building on the oldest supported image.** This prevents "GLIBC_2.38 not found" on users' machines.
7. **Reproducibility checked by an independent rebuild and digest compare.** It is cheap supply-chain assurance.
8. **Checksum lookup by exact filename, a symlink refusal, and an atomic temp-then-`mv` install.** These close common curl-pipe-sh pitfalls.
9. **Wall-clock timeouts on every download** (`timeout` wrapping wget). Installers then never hang in CI.
10. **Never edit PATH or rc files silently; print the exact command.** Users trust installers that don't touch their dotfiles.
11. **Documented source precedence (`--from` > env > pin > latest), printed in `--help`.** Behavior is predictable and the help text documents itself.
12. **`FGCTL_ASSET_BASE_URL` mirror override shared by the installer and the binary.** It covers air-gapped installs and test fixtures for free.
13. **Stable shim that reads an activation file, with tmp + fsync + rename writes.** Upgrades are atomic, and hook commands never change path.
14. **Doctor is read-only by default, with `--fix` and `--strict` (exit code), and checks live in a registry modules plug into.** One tool serves humans, CI and auto-repair.
15. **Setup and fixes are fill-only and idempotent, and report what changed.** They are safe to rerun and never clobber user customization.
16. **Uninstall needs `--yes`, reverses only what is still exactly as installed, and confirms package ownership before removing.** Nothing destructive happens by surprise.
17. **Config files hold only differences from a shipped standard, with `@fgos:why` reasons.** Upgrades change defaults cleanly and every override is explained.
18. **Scope annotations stop a committed project file from setting machine or secret keys.** Anyone who can land a commit could otherwise change machine settings, so this closes that hole.
19. **Embed the version manifest with `include_str!` and add a drift test plus a tag==version gate.** One version source holds across languages.
20. **One canonical skill source, generated per-agent wrappers, a doctor drift check, and project-local hooks only.** Multi-agent support stays consistent and never pollutes `~/`.

- **No authenticity, only integrity.** `SHA256SUMS` comes from the same origin as the tarballs, with no minisign, cosign, GPG or GitHub build provenance attestation.

## 3. Ideas worth copying

1. **Stamp the version into the installer at release time.** `latest/download/install.sh` then always matches its own release, and the copy in the repo can't silently install the wrong thing.
2. **Ownership marker file next to the binary.** It makes upgrades and uninstalls safe (an unmanaged binary is never touched) and gives self-update a source of truth for the version.
3. **Stage in the same directory, rename, run `version`, roll back.** Do this in the installer and in self-update; on Windows, use the `.old` rename for the running exe.
4. **Keyless cosign tied to the exact workflow and tag, verified inside the release job before publishing.** A broken signature never ships.
5. **Optional signature check that degrades loudly.** Print the exact verify command, offer `REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1`, and word the result to say whether the signature was actually checked.
6. **Byte caps and archive-shape checks on every download** (single member, regular file). Cheap protection against hostile mirrors.
7. **Reproducible builds:** commit-time date, `-trimpath -buildvcs=false`, deterministic tar and zip, sorted checksums.
8. **The release reruns the full CI as a reusable workflow,** so nothing ships without the same gate as main.
9. **Smoke-test the literal one-liner** on every OS after publishing, including upgrade from the previous release, PATH in a new login shell, and uninstall.
10. **Fixture mode with a fake verifier for installer tests,** making supply-chain logic testable offline.
11. **Fenced, removable profile blocks** (`# >>> app >>>`), with fish support and `ZDOTDIR` respected. Uninstall is then exact.
12. **Keep unknown keys when rewriting the config file,** so it stays compatible both forwards and backwards.
13. **Doctor with stable finding codes, a fix action per finding, `--fix --dry-run`, meaningful exit codes, and JSON output.**
14. **Edits to other tools' config files are planned with a preimage digest and surgical** (the user's formatting is kept), with `--dry-run` and `--remove`.
15. **A table of digests of everything ever shipped,** used to tell "our old file, safe to upgrade" from "user-edited, leave alone", and enforced by CI.
16. **One env var to redirect config** (`SKILLSTATION_USER_CONFIG_DIR`), so tests and smoke runs never touch the real user's config.

# Case study — mdview

## Shape
- Rust workspace: `mdview-core` (lib) + `mdview` (CLI). Desktop (Tauri) crate excluded from
  default members so the CLI never needs webview libs.
- One version: `[workspace.package] version`. Binary reads only `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")`.
- Release profile: `opt-level="s"`, `lto`, `codegen-units=1`, `panic="abort"`, `strip`.
- Front-end JS bundle (esbuild) is **committed** and embedded → Rust build never needs Node.

## Release
- Tag `v*` → matrix: `x86_64/aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` (via `cross`, static), `aarch64-apple-darwin`,
  `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. Intel mac dropped deliberately (scarce runner stalled releases).
- Asset = **bare binary named by target triple**: `mdview-<triple>[.exe]`, fetched via
  `releases/latest/download/<asset>` (no API call → no rate limit).
- `fail_on_unmatched_files: true`, `generate_release_notes: true`.

## Install (`install.sh`, `install.ps1`)
- POSIX `sh`, `set -eu`; `uname` → triple; unsupported → prints `cargo install` command.
- Install dir: first writable of `/usr/local/bin` → `~/.local/bin` → `~/.mdview/bin`; override `MDVIEW_INSTALL_DIR`; pin `MDVIEW_VERSION`.
- **Download beside target, rename over it** (avoids "Text file busy" while daemon runs).
- HTTP 200 → install; **404 → `cargo install --git` fallback; other → hard fail** (network errors never silently become source builds).
- Prints PATH hint (never edits rc files), runs `--version`, prints "Next:" commands (`doctor --fix`, …).
- Windows: rename running exe to `.old`, move new in.

## Self-update (`mdview update [--check] [--version vX] [--force]`)
- Repo from `env!("CARGO_PKG_REPOSITORY")` → forks update from themselves.
- Verify size + GitHub asset `sha256:` digest, then **smoke test**: staged binary must print exactly target version within 30s.
- Stage next to real binary (symlinks resolved) → atomic rename; Windows rename-aside `.old-<pid>` + rollback; every start cleans parked `.old*`.
- Downgrade policy is a **pure tested function** (`should_install`): only explicit `--version` pin downgrades.
- After swap, **runs the NEW binary by path** (`doctor --after-update`) so new embedded templates are installed; restarts daemon.
- sudo-aware: under sudo skips user-owned steps (daemon, skills) and tells the user what to run.
- Daemon auto-replaced when older (asks live process for version; never downgrades).
- MCP server is a thin per-call proxy to the CLI → updates apply without MCP reconnect.

## Config
- `~/.mdview/` (not XDG): `config.toml`, `registry-v4.db`, `daemon.lock`.
- `#[serde(default)]` everywhere; `#[serde(alias = "old_name")]` for renamed keys.
- `write_atomic` = temp in same dir + rename, **preserving existing file mode** (reused for third-party configs like 0600 `~/.claude.json`).
- **Schema version in DB filename** (`registry-v4.db`) → old/new binaries coexist during upgrade; doctor cleans legacy.
- `mdview config edit` → `$VISUAL`/`$EDITOR`/`vi`, re-validates after save.

## Doctor (`doctor [--fix] [--dry-run] [--json] [--mcp]`)
- Statuses `OK ✓ / FIXED + / MANUAL ! / WARN ~ / SKIP –`; `--json` output.
- Read-only diagnosis (SQLite opened read-only), asks live daemon for version.
- **Only configures agent tools that are actually installed** (else SKIP).

## Agent integration
- Managed block `<!-- mdview:START -->…<!-- mdview:END -->` upserted in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, writes through symlinks, exact-match = in sync. Template via `include_str!`, `.gitattributes` forces LF.
- Global skill `~/.claude/skills/mdview/SKILL.md` from embedded template; refreshed on update only if present.
- MCP registration for Claude Code / Codex (TOML via `toml_edit`, comments survive, malformed untouched) / Claude Desktop incl. **WSL → Windows Claude Desktop** via `wsl.exe -d <distro> -e <exe> mcp`. MCP is opt-in (`--mcp`).

## Uninstall (`uninstall [--purge] [-y] [--dry-run]`)
- **Plan → print → confirm → apply**; non-TTY refuses without `--yes`.
- Each step is the inverse of something `doctor --fix` created; re-reads config at apply time; timestamped backups.
- Irreversible steps (binary, data dir) skipped if any earlier step failed. Data kept unless `--purge`.
- Windows: deferred delete of running exe via detached `cmd`. Refuses under sudo.

## Gaps observed (do NOT copy)
- Installers verify no checksum; no `SHA256SUMS`, no signing/attestation.
- Release not gated on CI; no tag==Cargo version check; manual bump; no CHANGELOG.
- Doctor always exits 0 (useless in CI); `check_config` writes without `--fix`.
- Unparseable JSON treated as `{}` and overwritten when registering MCP.
- Daemon default bind `0.0.0.0` + token `demo`.
- No shell completions / man pages; no XDG / `*_HOME` override.

---
project: vantt/herdr-go
language: rust (+ Vite/TS web UI embedded)
kind: long-running user service (web gateway) + CLI + herdr plugin
channels: [github-releases-archives, checksums.txt, install.sh, install.ps1, self-update, herdr-plugin-marketplace]
distilled: 2026-11-02 (v0.1.22)
---

# Case study — herdr-go

## Shape
- Single Rust binary (axum/tokio/rusqlite bundled/reqwest+rustls) with Vite web UI embedded via `rust-embed`.
- `build.rs` creates `static/` so a fresh checkout compiles without npm; on-disk `index.html` overrides embedded (doctor reports which).
- **Version fingerprint** from `build.rs`: `0.1.22 (abc123-dirty, <timestamp>)` exposed on `/api/health`; no `rerun-if` → never stale; `nogit` fallback.

## Release
- `scripts/release.sh [--dry-run] [--yes]`: on `main`, clean tree, HEAD == origin/main, tag absent, version check passes, CI status via `gh api …/check-runs`, then confirm "irreversible" → tag/push.
- Matrix: musl x86_64/aarch64 (cross), aarch64-apple-darwin, windows msvc. **Pinned runner images** (never `-latest`).
- Archive `herdr-go-<triple>.tar.gz|.zip` contains binary, `config.example.json`, installer, README, service unit/plist, docs.
- **`checksums.txt` produced by a job that `needs:` every build** → partial releases have no checksums → updater fails closed.
- **Post-release smoke tests on real assets**: Windows (install → Scheduled Task → crash-restart → uninstall), macOS (LaunchAgent), and **update-from-previous-tag** (previous tag resolved dynamically, asserts `/api/health` version changed). Third-party binaries in CI are hash-pinned.

## Version discipline
- `scripts/check-version.sh` + `.githooks/pre-commit`: code change without version bump is blocked; versions monotonic (`sort -V`); `herdr-plugin.toml` must match `Cargo.toml`. Bypass `SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1`.
- `ci` mode compares with latest tag; `drift` mode emits a non-failing "release may be overdue" note.

## Install
- `install.sh [--uninstall]`, `PREFIX` (default `~/.local`), pin `HERDR_GO_VERSION`; `curl -fSL --proto '=https'` into `mktemp -d` + trap.
- OS-native paths, commented "MUST match `src/config/mod.rs`" (XDG on Linux, Application Support on macOS, Known Folders on Windows).
- **Preflight** before touching anything (launchctl present / `systemctl --user show-environment` works).
- Legacy-dir migration that **fails closed if both old and new exist**.
- **Default config generated by the binary itself**: `herdr-go --internal-print-default-config > config.json` (only if absent).
- Secret token in `herdr-go.env` with `umask 077`/`chmod 600`; printed only on first creation. On Windows the **binary** creates it with owner-only DACL (PowerShell would inherit ACEs the binary's own check rejects).
- Idempotent service registration: `bootout` before `bootstrap`; disables conflicting legacy/dev units.

## Service
- `herdr-go service start|stop|restart|status` → thin passthrough to systemd --user / launchctl / Scheduled Task.
- systemd hardening: `NoNewPrivileges`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ReadWritePaths=…`, `Restart=always`; `loginctl enable-linger`.
- Unit files contain no secrets (binary reads its own env file).
- `dev-deploy.sh` installs a **separate dev unit** from a template (`@REPO@` placeholders) and stops prod.

## Self-update
- GitHub API latest → semver compare → asset name mirrors installer mapping → download + `checksums.txt`, **fail closed** on missing file/entry/mismatch.
- Rollout: stop service → backup `<exe>.bak-<nanos>` → atomic swap → **run NEW binary `--internal-merge-config`** (add-missing-keys-only merge, validates before write) → start → poll `/api/health` → **auto-rollback binary + config** on failure.

## Config
- JSON, `deny_unknown_fields`, collects all validation errors at once. **No secrets in config.**
- Secret precedence: env `HERDR_GO_WEB_SECRET` → `herdr-go.env` (must pass permission check: mode `&0o077==0` and owner==euid / owner-only DACL) → generate new (`create_new`, 0600).
- Zero-config start: auto-creates sensible defaults.
- Legacy migration only on default-config normal startup, not for doctor/demo/explicit `--config` (mode-matrix test).
- `-b/--bind` non-loopback prints a security notice.

## Doctor
- Checks with `ok|fail|info|skipped`, each carries `critical` + `fix` hint.
- Phases: diagnose → (TTY) guided fixes → **re-run all checks so exit code reflects post-fix state** → optional settings editor.
- `--check` or non-TTY = read-only; exit 0 only if all critical checks pass.

## Uninstall
- Removes service + binary only; **always keeps config/data/token and says so**; manual purge steps documented.

## Plugin manifest (`herdr-plugin.toml`)
- Thin launcher: `min_herdr_version`, platforms, only **read-only actions** (`service status`, `url`) — start/stop intentionally excluded.

## Docs / tests
- `docs/specs/*` with numbered decisions cited from code comments.
- `tests/rename_contract.sh`: static contract test cross-checking asset names across workflow/installers/docs, links, unit hardening.

## Gaps observed (do NOT copy)
- `update` writes the **archive bytes** over the executable (no extraction) — archive vs. raw-binary mismatch between release and updater. Lesson: test updater against real release assets.
- Installers don't verify `checksums.txt`; installers run from raw `main` while binary may be pinned tag (version skew).
- macOS uninstall hint points to a URL not published as a release asset.
- No PATH handling; inconsistent first-run behavior across OSes; 3 drifting copies of default config.
- Assets published before smoke tests (no draft → promote).
- `.bak-<nanos>` never cleaned; contract test & githooks not wired into CI / `core.hooksPath`.

The product ships a tiny bootstrap binary, `fgctl`. `fgctl` downloads a release tree, checks its digest and activates it for one project.
